paragraphs.source_en: The rest of the lecture was still very long. According to his original plan, Kangetsu had intended to go on and discuss the physiological effects of hanging, but Meitei kept inserting all sorts of rambling odd remarks along the way, and the master, too, yawned from time to time without the least restraint, so Kangetsu was forced to beat a retreat halfway through, take his leave, and go. What manner Kangetsu adopted that evening, and how he unfolded his eloquence, I naturally have no way of knowing, since it was something that took place far away.

paragraphs.source_en: After that, two or three days passed uneventfully. One day, around two o’clock in the afternoon, Meitei again drifted in, as usual, as airily as some child of chance. As soon as he sat down, he asked the master, “Say, have you heard about Ochi Tofu’s Takanawa affair?” His manner had all the urgency of someone arriving to announce an extra edition reporting the fall of Port Arthur. “No. I haven’t seen him lately.” The master answered listlessly, just as usual. “Today, despite being busy, I have come expressly to report to you the story of Brother Tofu’s disgrace.” The master said, “There you go exaggerating again. You really are a lawless fellow.” Meitei said, “Ha ha... don’t call it lawless; I am merely somewhat disorderly in talk. I must ask you to distinguish that point, or my honor is at stake.” The master, a pure reincarnation of Tennen Koji, said with utter indifference, “Isn’t it the same thing?” Meitei was itching to tell his news: “They say Brother Tofu went to Sengakuji in Takanawa last Sunday. On a cold day like this, he would have done better to stay at home. Quite apart from anything else, going to Sengakuji nowadays makes one look like a country bumpkin visiting Tokyo for the first time, doesn’t it?” “That is Tofu’s own affair. You have no right to stop him.” Meitei said, “True, I have no right. That is beside the point. You know the exhibition there in the temple called the Society for the Preservation of Loyal Retainers’ Relics, don’t you?” The master answered, “I don’t.” Meitei said, “What? You don’t know it? But surely you have at least been to Sengakuji?” “No.” “Never? Well, that is astonishing; no wonder you have been defending Tofu all along. For an Edo man like you never to have been to Sengakuji is really rather shameful.” “Even without having been there, I can still serve as a teacher.” The more the master spoke, the more fully he took on the manner of Tennen Koji. Meitei said, “Let that pass; let us return to Tofu. He went into that exhibition room to look around, and just then a German husband and wife came in. At first, they apparently asked Tofu something in Japanese, but this gentleman, as usual, was simply dying to try out his German, so he rattled off two or three sentences in German, and to his surprise they came out rather well. Thinking back afterward, that was precisely where the trouble began.” “And what happened then?” asked the master. At last he had been drawn into Meitei’s trap. “They say the German saw Otaka Gengo’s maki-e lacquer seal case and said he wanted to buy it, asking whether they would sell it to him. Tofu’s answer at the time was quite splendid: ‘The Japanese are all upright gentlemen, so it is certainly impossible.’ Those few sentences in German were fairly fluent, so the German thought he had found a good interpreter and began asking him question after question.” The master said, “What did he ask?” “That is just the trouble. If he could understand it, there would have been no difficulty. The German spoke extremely fast, and whenever he asked a question it came in a whole string, so Tofu could not make out what he was saying at all. Now and then he could catch a phrase or two, but the questions were all about fire hooks and mallets, and since he had never learned those German words, of course he had no idea how to translate them. That left him in a terrible fix.”

paragraphs.source_zh: 此后两三天太平无事地过去。一天，午后两点左右，迷亭又照例像偶然童子似的，飘然而来。他一就坐，立刻问主人道：“喂，你听说越智东风的高轮事件了吗？”他那神态大有来报告旅顺陷落号外的架势。“不知道。最近我没见着他。”主人还和平素一样，无精打采地回答说。“我今天不顾繁忙，特地是来向你报告东风老兄丢人故事的哩。”主人说：“又是那样夸大其辞，你真是个胡闹的家伙。”迷亭说：“哈哈……不要说什么胡闹吧，我不过是好胡扯而已。这点请你务必区分开，否则关系到我的名誉呢。”主人纯粹是个天然居士再生，满不理会地说：“还不是一样？”迷亭巴不得讲他的消息：“据说上星期天东风老兄去高轮的泉岳寺了，这样冷的天，呆在家里多好。甭说别的，现在去什么泉岳寺，岂不让人看成是第一次来东京的乡巴佬吗？”“那随东风君的便，你没权利阻挡他。”迷亭说：“不错，我是没权利。这没关系。你知道那庙里有个‘义士遗物保存会’的展览吧？”主人答道：“不知道。”迷亭说：“什么？你不知道？那泉岳寺你总去过吧？”“没有。”“没有？这可真令人吃惊，怪不得你一直替东风辩护哩。你这个江户儿竟然没去过泉岳寺，未免太丢人了吧。”“没去过，我也照样当教师嘛。”主人越说越以“天然居士”自居起来。迷亭说：“且不管这个，先说东风吧，他进入那个展览室去参观，正赶上来了一对德国夫妇，据说他们最初是用日语向东风打听什么，可是这位老兄，正急不可耐地想试试自己的德语，于是就说了两三句德国话，想不到还说得蛮漂亮。事后一想，问题就出在这点上。”“那么后来怎样啦？”主人问道。他终于被陷进迷亭设下的圈套。“据说德国人看见了大高源吾的描金漆印盒，说他想买，问能否卖给他。当时东风回答得非常妙：‘日本人都是清廉的君子，肯定不会卖的。’这几句德语说得还满流利，那德国人以为碰上了一位好翻译，于是接二连三地向他发问。”主人说：“都问了些什么？”“问题就在这里呢，若是能听懂，也就用不着为难啦。那德国人说得非常快，而且一问就是一大串问题，根本摸不清他说的是什么。其中偶尔也能听懂一两句，可是问的又都是关于消防钩、榔头的事，他没学过德语中这些词汇，当然不知道怎么译才好。这下他可犯难了。”
